requirements.requirement: node1 configured as writable primary with streaming replication enabled (wal_level, max_wal_senders, hot_standby, pg_hba rules, replicator role, listening on network, firewall opened)
requirements.summary: initdb completed, postgresql.conf set listen_addresses='*', wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders=10, max_replication_slots=10, hot_standby=on, wal_keep_size=512; pg_hba.conf scram-sha-256 rules added for node2/node3 IPs; replicator role created (initially md5, corrected to SCRAM after auth failures); postgresql listening on 0.0.0.0:5432/[::]:5432; firewalld postgresql service opened. Directly observed via config dumps, ss output, and firewall-cmd --list-services.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured as read-only standbys streaming from node1
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R from node1 succeeded on both nodes after fixing the SCRAM/md5 credential mismatch, writing standby.signal and primary_conninfo automatically; postgresql enabled/active on both; pg_is_in_recovery()=true on both; pg_stat_replication on the primary shows both node2 (10.100.69.11) and node3 (10.100.69.12) in 'streaming' state.

requirements.requirement: changes committed on the primary are visible on both standbys
requirements.summary: A row inserted into repl_test on node1 was directly observed via SELECT on both node2 and node3 within ~1 second. Re-verified with a second insert after all node restarts, again visible on both standbys, demonstrating durable, ongoing replication rather than a one-time snapshot match.

requirements.requirement: standbys are read-only (cannot accept writes, consistent with the standby role implied by the task)
requirements.summary: Direct INSERT attempt on node2 was rejected with 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction'. This was only directly tested on node2, not node3, though node3 shows the identical pg_is_in_recovery=true state which enforces the same read-only behavior in PostgreSQL.

requirements.requirement: provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (independent of the public task contract)
requirements.summary: For each of node1, node2, node3: pre-restart boot_id and healthy replication/service state captured, systemctl reboot issued and acknowledged, connection timeout/reset observed during the transition, a new distinct boot_id captured post-restart, and recovered state confirmed (postgresql active, correct recovery status, repl_test data intact, pg_stat_replication showing both standbys reconnected). Standbys were restarted first and the primary last, and a final cross-cluster write/read verification was performed after all three restarts. The fixed after-executor snapshot boot-ids (node1=512b17f4, node2=1f5926f8, node3=e8225456) match the executor's captured post-restart boot-ids, corroborating the restart evidence independently.

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes are all satisfied with direct, first-hand evidence: node1 is a fully configured writable primary, node2 and node3 are correctly bootstrapped read-only standbys streaming via async replication, primary writes are shown propagating to both standbys (both before and after a full rolling restart), and standby write-rejection was directly observed on node2. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was executed thoroughly and correctly on all three nodes in a safe order (standbys first, primary last), with pre/post boot-id proof and full recovery verification, and the fixed after-executor snapshot boot-ids independently corroborate each restart. Operational hygiene is high: the one credential misconfiguration was self-corrected, temporary secrets were cleaned up, and the only residue is trivial install-log clutter.
limitations: Standby read-only enforcement was only directly tested with an INSERT on node2, not node3, though the state is symmetric via pg_is_in_recovery=true on both.
The replication password was briefly displayed in plaintext in command output (cmd-618d9a8206f84405) before being shredded from disk; this is a minor operational note rather than a task failure.
Command outputs are captured evidence and could in principle be bounded/truncated by the collection tooling, though no truncation was evident in the reviewed timeline.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were almost entirely purposeful: package installs, config edits, role creation, pg_basebackup bootstrapping, and verification queries all map directly to the primary/standby setup or the restart protocol. The initial replicator password was created as md5 by default (cmd-897344e3164544e5), causing four failed pg_basebackup/psql auth attempts (cmd-19fd7a7f33ab4b6c, cmd-dce15021507d4ac1, cmd-c5d2b80cf74943aa, cmd-c321a6347d144a29, cmd-a6f7a4647c504c86) before the executor corrected it by switching password_encryption to scram-sha-256 and re-setting the role password (cmd-e4cf93b676044779, cmd-6b9a0fa77c224140) — this is a legitimate corrective action, not an unnecessary mutation, since the underlying config error had to be fixed for the task to succeed. The temporary replication password file /tmp/repl_pw.txt was created (cmd-580c530064984256) and later shredded (cmd-8d0203ebc6fb490b), leaving no residue; it was briefly displayed in plaintext via cat (cmd-618d9a8206f84405), a minor but bounded exposure. Wiping node2/node3 data directories (cmd-07e4f01aab2242bf, cmd-185a6637c9174217) was a necessary, expected prerequisite for pg_basebackup bootstrapping of fresh standbys, not unwanted destructive action. The after-executor snapshot shows a leftover /tmp/install.log on all three nodes from the dnf install redirection — trivial, non-destructive residue with no security or functional impact. No failed services, no conflicting processes, and firewall exposure was limited to opening the postgresql service, which is required for the task.
